abstract:
Diet rich in fat, such as high-fat diet (HFD) and ketogenic diet (KD), has complex impacts on immunity. Neutrophils adapt to tissue-specific signals and exert innate defense functions against infections and malignancies. However, whether and how dietary fat shapes tissue-specific neutrophil functions remains unclear. This study aims at determining the effect of dietary fat on tissue-specific pulmonary antitumor responses mediated by neutrophils.
Mouse models of HFD or KD feeding, in combination with a lung metastatic B16 melanoma or a primary Lewis lung carcinoma lung cancer model, were used to determine the impact of dietary fat on pulmonary tissue-specific reprogramming of antitumor functions in neutrophils. A multitude of experimental approaches were used to address the mechanisms through which HFD/KD boosts antitumor functions of intrapulmonary neutrophils. We also performed correlation analysis between immune activation signatures in human lung cancer-infiltrating neutrophils and serum lipids, and analyzed published single-cell transcription data in human lungs, to determine the potential correlation between serum lipid contents or endothelial cell-derived signals and antitumor functions of lung neutrophils.
Both HFD-fed and KD-fed mice demonstrated enhanced neutrophil-mediated pulmonary tumor resistance compared with chow diet-fed mice, in either a prophylactic or a therapeutic setting. Intrapulmonary, but not systemic, neutrophils in HFD/KD-fed mice exhibited enhanced potential for reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and ROS-dependent tumor cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, HFD/KD-induced increased serum palmitic acid (PA) and cholesterol stimulate lung vascular endothelial cells (LVECs), which reprogram neutrophils via contact-dependent and intercellular adhesion molecule-1-dependent mechanisms. In humans, increased serum cholesterol levels are associated with increased myeloperoxidase contents in lung cancer-infiltrating neutrophils, and intensified adhesion and priming signals from human LVECs are potentially associated with immune activation in intrapulmonary neutrophils.
These data suggest that dietary fat boosts lung tissue-specific antitumor immunity mediated by neutrophils with an enhanced potential for ROS production, which are primed by LVECs stimulated by elevated serum PA and cholesterol. Our findings highlight the roles of dietary fats in shaping neutrophil functions in a tissue-specific manner. Dietary intervention targeting tissue-specific reprogramming of neutrophils, therefore, represents a potential strategy against malignancies in the lungs.
